ai_sections.title: Transformer Losses and Efficiency
pyq_focus: 2025–26 Q6 · practical transformer: equivalent circuit, efficiency and regulation (10M)
paragraphs: A transformer has no mechanical rotation, so the important losses for this unit are winding copper loss and iron/core loss.
Copper loss changes with load current, whereas iron loss is treated as approximately constant when the applied voltage and frequency are constant.

formulae.label: Copper loss at x p.u. load

ai_sections.key_point: For efficiency questions, first separate the load-dependent copper loss from the nearly constant iron loss; maximum efficiency occurs when the two are equal.

study_groups.heading: Losses in a transformer
bullets: Primary copper loss is \(I_1^2R_1\) and secondary copper loss is \(I_2^2R_2\). Hence copper loss is current-dependent and varies with load.
At \(x\) per-unit load, current is \(x\) times full-load current, so copper loss becomes \(x^2W_{cu,FL}\). Thus half-load copper loss is one-quarter of full-load copper loss.
Iron or magnetic loss consists mainly of hysteresis loss and eddy-current loss in the core.
At constant applied voltage and frequency, the core flux is approximately constant; hence iron loss \(W_i\) is treated as a constant loss with respect to load.

formulae.label: Copper loss at x p.u. load

study_groups.heading: Efficiency — exam-ready derivation
steps: Refer the quantities to the primary side and write the transformer input power as \(P_{in}=V_1I_1\cos\phi\).
Write total loss as the sum of variable copper loss and constant iron loss: \(W_L=I_1^2R_{01}+W_i\).
Useful output is input minus losses: \(P_{out}=P_{in}-W_L\).
Substitute in \(\eta=P_{out}/P_{in}\) and multiply by 100 for percentage efficiency.

study_groups.heading: Condition for maximum efficiency
steps: In the efficiency expression, iron loss is the constant loss while copper loss varies with load current.
Maximizing efficiency gives the standard condition that variable copper loss equals constant iron loss.
Therefore \(I_1^2R_{01}=W_i\). In load-fraction form, \(x^2W_{cu,FL}=W_i\).
If full-load copper loss is known, the load fraction for maximum efficiency is \(x=\sqrt{W_i/W_{cu,FL}}\).

ai_sections.title: Basic Construction of a DC Machine
paragraphs: A DC generator and a DC motor use the same basic machine construction. The direction of energy conversion changes, but the main parts remain the same.
Before studying generator and motor action, identify which parts stay stationary and which parts rotate.

formulae.label: Parallel paths
formulae.latex: A=P\text{ for lap winding},\qquad A=2\text{ for wave winding}

ai_sections.key_point: Remember the machine in two groups: field system (yoke, poles, field coils) and armature system (armature, commutator, brushes).

study_groups.heading: Read the machine construction first
paragraphs: The construction drawing below is the map for the rest of Unit III. The stationary field system produces magnetic flux; the rotating armature carries the conductors in which emf is induced or on which force acts.

diagrams.title: Basic Construction of a DC Machine
diagrams.alt: Figure 3.31 · Basic Construction of a DC Machine · Textbook p. 163
diagrams.teaching_note: Read the drawing from outside to inside. The yoke is the outer magnetic frame; the pole cores and pole shoes carry the field coils and create the stationary magnetic field. The armature is the rotating part inside the field. Its conductors are connected to the commutator, which rotates with the armature, while the carbon brushes remain stationary and carry current between the rotating armature and the external circuit.
diagrams.caption: Basic construction of a DC machine

study_groups.heading: One construction, two energy-conversion modes
paragraphs: A DC generator and a DC motor use the same basic machine construction. In generator operation the machine converts mechanical energy to electrical energy; in motor operation it converts electrical energy to mechanical energy.

study_groups.heading: Stator / field-system parts
bullets: Yoke: the outer frame. It gives mechanical support and also provides a return path for magnetic flux.
Pole cores and pole shoes: carry the main magnetic flux. Pole shoes spread the flux over the air gap and support the field coils; the pole structure is laminated to reduce eddy-current loss.
Field windings: copper windings placed on the poles and supplied with DC excitation to produce the main magnetic field.

study_groups.heading: Rotor / armature-system parts
bullets: Armature core: a laminated silicon-steel rotating core with slots. It houses the armature conductors and provides a low-reluctance magnetic path.
Armature winding: the interconnected armature conductors in which generated emf appears and through which armature current flows.
Commutator: the segmented rotating electrical connection associated with the armature winding.
Brushes: stationary carbon/graphite contacts resting on the commutator; they provide the electrical connection between the rotating armature and the external circuit.

study_groups.heading: Armature winding and parallel paths
bullets: In a lap winding, the number of armature parallel paths is equal to the number of poles: \(A=P\).
In a wave winding, the number of parallel paths is \(A=2\).
This value of \(A\) is important in the DC-generator and back-emf equations.

ai_sections.title: DC Generator Principle and EMF Equation
pyq_focus: 2025–26 Q5(b) · derive the DC-generator EMF equation (5M)
2023–24 Q6(a) · generator EMF derivation (5M)
paragraphs: A DC generator converts mechanical energy into electrical energy by electromagnetic induction. When armature conductors move through the magnetic field and cut flux, an emf is induced; Fleming’s right-hand rule gives the induced-current direction.

The sequence is easiest to understand in three stages: first see why a rotating loop naturally produces alternating emf, then see how the commutator makes the external current unidirectional, and finally use pole pitch to derive the generated armature emf.
ai_sections.key_point: Follow the pictures in order: rotating loop + slip rings explain the alternating induced output; the split-ring commutator explains unidirectional external current; the pole-pitch picture supplies the distance/flux step used to derive \(E_g=P\Phi ZN/(60A)\).

study_groups.heading: Simple loop: why the induced output alternates
paragraphs: Start with one rectangular coil ABCD rotating between the N and S poles. As the active conductors cut magnetic flux, an emf is induced in the coil.

The coil ends are connected to two continuous slip rings. Stationary brushes press on these rings and connect the rotating coil to the external load R. In the drawing, M and N are the two external load-side terminals, so a statement such as “current flows from M to N” simply tells you the direction of current through the load.

After half a revolution, the direction of induced emf in the coil reverses. Because the slip-ring connections themselves do not swap, the current direction through the external load also reverses. This is therefore an alternating-emf stage, not yet a DC output.
bullets: N, S: magnetic poles that establish the field.
ABCD: the rotating armature loop.
Slip rings: continuous rings connected to the two coil ends; they rotate with the coil.
Brushes: stationary contacts that collect current from the rotating rings.
R: external load; M and N identify its two connection terminals.

diagrams.title: Simple Loop Generator
diagrams.alt: Figure 3.26 · Simple Loop Generator showing the rotating coil, continuous slip rings, brushes and external load R between terminals M and N · Textbook p. 161
diagrams.teaching_note: In this simple-loop generator, N and S are the magnetic poles and ABCD is the rotating coil. The coil ends connect to continuous slip rings, which rotate with the coil. The stationary brushes collect the induced current and feed the external load R. The labels M and N mark the two external load-side terminals; current through the load is described by its direction from one terminal to the other. Because continuous slip rings do not reverse the external connections, the polarity at the brushes reverses every half-turn, so the output of this stage is alternating.
diagrams.caption: Simple loop generator: rotating coil, slip rings, brushes and external load

study_groups.heading: Commutator: how the external current becomes unidirectional
bullets: The continuous slip rings are replaced by two insulated commutator segments connected to the two ends of the coil.
The commutator rotates with the armature; the brushes remain stationary.
After every half-turn, the commutator segments exchange brush contact at the same instant that the coil emf reverses.
Therefore the brush connected to each external terminal keeps the same polarity, and current through the external load remains unidirectional.
paragraphs: A DC generator must keep the current through the external load in one direction even though the emf induced in the rotating coil reverses every half-turn.

diagrams.title: Action of Commutator
diagrams.alt: Figure 3.29 · Action of Commutator showing the split-ring segments changing brush contact over successive half-turns so the load current remains unidirectional · Textbook p. 162
diagrams.teaching_note: Now replace the two continuous slip rings with a split-ring commutator. Each half of the commutator is connected to one end of the rotating coil. Every half-turn, the coil emf reverses and the commutator simultaneously swaps which coil end touches each stationary brush. These two reversals cancel at the external terminals, so the load current continues in the same direction.
diagrams.caption: Action of the split-ring commutator

study_groups.heading: EMF equation: derive it from one pole pitch
steps: Let \(P\) = number of poles, \(\Phi\) = flux per pole in webers, \(Z\) = total armature conductors, \(N\) = speed in rpm, and \(A\) = number of parallel paths.
From the pole-pitch drawing, when one conductor moves from one pole centre to the next, it crosses one pole pitch and cuts one pole flux, so flux cut = \(\Phi\) Wb.
At \(N\) rpm, one revolution takes \(60/N\) s. One revolution contains \(P\) pole pitches, so time to move through one pole pitch is \(60/(NP)\) s.
Average emf induced in one conductor is therefore \(e=\Phi/[60/(NP)]=\Phi NP/60\) V.
Each parallel path contains \(Z/A\) armature conductors in series.
Hence the generated armature emf is \(E_g=e(Z/A)=P\Phi ZN/(60A)\).
paragraphs: Once the commutation idea is clear, the generated-emf equation follows from how much flux one conductor cuts while moving through one pole pitch.

diagrams.title: conductor passing through a Pole pitch
diagrams.alt: Figure 3.35 · conductor passing through a Pole pitch · Textbook p. 166
diagrams.teaching_note: This drawing supplies the geometric step used in the EMF equation. One pole pitch is the distance, measured around the armature, from the centre of one pole to the centre of the next pole. When one armature conductor moves through one pole pitch, it cuts the flux of one pole, \(\Phi\). With \(P\) poles and speed \(N\) rpm, the conductor crosses \(P\) pole pitches per revolution, giving the time for one pole pitch as \(60/(NP)\) s.
diagrams.caption: One conductor moving through one pole pitch

study_groups.heading: Choose the correct number of parallel paths
bullets: Lap winding: \(A=P\).
Wave winding: \(A=2\).
Always identify the armature winding before substituting in the EMF equation.

ai_sections.caution: On textbook p. 161 the running text names Fleming’s Left Hand Rule while discussing generator-induced current; the generator direction rule used here is Fleming’s Right Hand Rule, consistent with the generator treatment elsewhere in the chapter.

ai_sections.title: DC Motor Principle and Back EMF
pyq_focus: 2025–26 Part A(c) · significance of back EMF (2M)
2023–24 Q6(b) · working of a DC motor with diagram (5M)
paragraphs: A DC motor converts electrical energy into mechanical energy. A current-carrying conductor placed in a magnetic field experiences a force; forces on opposite armature conductors form a torque and rotate the armature.
As the armature rotates, its conductors also cut flux and generate an emf. By Lenz’s law this generated emf opposes the applied voltage and is therefore called back emf \(E_b\).
ai_sections.key_point: Back emf is essential to normal motor operation: it opposes the supply, rises with speed, and automatically changes armature current as speed and load change.

study_groups.heading: Motor principle
paragraphs: A DC motor converts electrical energy into mechanical energy. Its basic operating principle is the force on a current-carrying conductor placed in a magnetic field.

The figure below ties the three directions together: magnetic field, conductor current and the resulting force. Once the force on opposite armature conductors forms a couple, the armature develops torque.
bullets: For a conductor at right angles to the field, the force magnitude is written \(F=BIl\).
Fleming’s left-hand rule gives the direction of force.
In the textbook notation, \(\otimes\) means current flowing away from the reader and \(\odot\) means current flowing towards the reader.
Forces on conductors on opposite sides of the armature form a turning moment, so the armature rotates.

diagrams.title: Fleming’s Left Hand Rule
diagrams.alt: Figure 3.42 · Fleming’s Left Hand Rule showing magnetic field, conductor current and force directions · Textbook p. 172
diagrams.teaching_note: Read the three directions together: the forefinger represents the magnetic-field direction, the middle finger the conductor-current direction, and the thumb the resulting force or motion. This is the direction rule used in the motor-principle explanation above.
diagrams.caption: Fleming’s left-hand rule for motor force direction

study_groups.heading: Origin of back emf
bullets: Once the armature rotates, its conductors also cut magnetic flux.
The rotating armature therefore has generator action and develops an emf in the armature winding.
By Lenz’s law this generated emf opposes the applied supply voltage; hence it is called back emf \(E_b\).
The back-emf magnitude has the same form as the generated-emf equation of a DC generator.
paragraphs: The back-emf figure shows the second action occurring at the same time as motor action: while current in the armature produces torque, the rotating armature also cuts flux and therefore generates an emf of its own.

diagrams.title: Back Emf
diagrams.alt: Figure 3.44 · Back Emf in a rotating DC motor armature · Textbook p. 173
diagrams.teaching_note: The rotating armature behaves like a generator while it is acting as a motor. In the drawing, \(\otimes\) means current away from the reader and \(\odot\) means current towards the reader. The emf generated by this rotation is directed so that it opposes the applied armature voltage; that opposing emf is \(E_b\).
diagrams.caption: Back emf produced by the rotating armature

study_groups.heading: Why back emf is important
bullets: At starting, speed is zero, so \(E_b=0\). The armature current is then limited mainly by the small armature resistance.
As speed rises, \(E_b\) rises because \(E_b\propto N\). The opposing emf reduces the net voltage driving armature current.
If mechanical load increases, speed tends to fall; \(E_b\) falls and armature current rises.
Since motor torque is proportional to \(\Phi I_a\), the increased armature current produces more torque to meet the increased load.

ai_sections.title: Load Characteristics of a Separately Excited DC Motor
paragraphs: In a separately excited DC motor, the field winding has an independent supply, so the field current and flux can be held approximately constant while armature load changes.

formulae.label: Torque
formulae.latex: T\propto\Phi I_a\;\Rightarrow\;T\propto I_a\text{ when }\Phi\text{ is constant}

ai_sections.key_point: With separate excitation and nearly constant flux, torque follows armature current while speed decreases only slightly as load increases.

study_groups.heading: Why “separately excited” matters
paragraphs: The field winding has an independent supply. Therefore field current and magnetic flux can be kept approximately constant while the armature load is varied.

study_groups.heading: Torque versus armature current
bullets: Developed torque is proportional to the product of flux and armature current: \(T\propto\Phi I_a\).
With approximately constant flux, \(T\propto I_a\).
The torque–armature-current characteristic is therefore approximately a straight line.
paragraphs: Read the graph together with the torque equation: the nearly straight rising line is what the constant-flux relation \(T\propto I_a\) looks like.

diagrams.title: Torque vs Armature Current Characteristics
diagrams.alt: Figure 3.52 · Torque vs Armature Current Characteristics · Textbook p. 179
diagrams.teaching_note: Because the field flux is held approximately constant, torque follows armature current almost directly. The graph is therefore the visual form of \(T\propto I_a\): increasing load current produces an almost proportional increase in torque.
diagrams.caption: Torque versus armature current at nearly constant flux

study_groups.heading: Speed versus armature current
bullets: The motor voltage relation gives \(E_b=V-I_aR_a\).
Since \(E_b\propto\Phi N\), speed varies as \(N\propto(V-I_aR_a)/\Phi\).
With \(V\) and \(\Phi\) approximately constant, increasing armature current increases the \(I_aR_a\) drop, so speed falls slightly as load increases.
paragraphs: The next graph shows the small speed drop predicted by the voltage equation as armature current increases.

diagrams.title: Speed vs Armature Current Characteristics
diagrams.alt: Figure 3.53 · Speed vs Armature Current Characteristics · Textbook p. 180
diagrams.teaching_note: As armature current rises, the internal drop \(I_aR_a\) rises. With supply voltage and field flux approximately constant, the back emf and hence the speed fall slightly, giving the gently drooping characteristic shown.
diagrams.caption: Speed versus armature current for a separately excited motor

study_groups.heading: Speed versus torque
bullets: With constant flux, torque is proportional to armature current.
Therefore the speed–torque characteristic has the same gently falling trend as the speed–armature-current characteristic.
The separately excited motor is consequently treated as a nearly constant-speed motor over its normal load range.
paragraphs: Since torque and armature current track one another at constant flux, the speed–torque graph has the same gently falling shape.

diagrams.title: Speed vs Torque Characteristics
diagrams.alt: Figure 3.54 · Speed vs Torque Characteristics · Textbook p. 180
diagrams.teaching_note: At nearly constant flux, torque is approximately proportional to armature current. Replacing the current axis by torque therefore gives the same nearly constant-speed behaviour: speed decreases only slightly as torque increases.
diagrams.caption: Speed versus torque for a separately excited motor

ai_sections.title: Speed Control of a Separately Excited DC Motor
pyq_focus: 2023–24 Part A(c) · list DC-motor speed-control techniques (2M)
paragraphs: The speed relation shows two textbook control routes: vary the field flux, or insert a series control resistance in the armature circuit to change the voltage available to the armature.
ai_sections.key_point: Field control (flux weakening) → above rated speed. Armature control with a series rheostat → below rated speed.

study_groups.heading: Starting point — the speed equation
paragraphs: For a separately excited motor, the field circuit and armature circuit can be adjusted independently. The speed relation shows how each control method works.

study_groups.heading: Field control method
bullets: Keep the armature supply voltage essentially constant and vary the field current using a rheostat in the field circuit.
Increasing field-circuit resistance reduces field current and hence reduces flux \(\Phi\).
Since speed is inversely proportional to flux, weakening the field raises the speed; this method is used for speeds above rated speed.
The field circuit must not be allowed to open while the motor is running, because very small flux can produce dangerously high speed.
paragraphs: The circuit below shows exactly where the control element is placed: in the field branch. That placement is what makes this a flux-control method.

diagrams.title: Field Control Method
diagrams.alt: Figure 3.56 · Field Control Method · Textbook p. 182
diagrams.teaching_note: The field rheostat is in the separately excited field circuit, not in the armature circuit. Increasing its resistance reduces field current and weakens the flux. From \(N\propto 1/\Phi\), weakening the field raises the motor speed.
diagrams.caption: Field-control method for speeds above rated speed

study_groups.heading: Armature control method
bullets: Keep field current, and hence flux, approximately constant.
Insert a speed-control rheostat \(R_c\) in series with the armature circuit, as in Figure 3.58.
Part of the supply voltage is dropped across \(R_c\), so the voltage available across the armature decreases.
With flux constant, reducing effective armature voltage reduces speed; this method is used for speeds below rated speed.
paragraphs: In the armature-control circuit, the series rheostat is moved to the armature path. The field branch is left essentially unchanged, so the reduction in speed comes from reducing the voltage available to the armature.

diagrams.title: Armature Control Method
diagrams.alt: Figure 3.58 · Armature Control Method · Textbook p. 183
diagrams.teaching_note: Here the control rheostat is in series with the armature while the field current is kept approximately constant. The rheostat takes part of the supply voltage, so the effective armature voltage falls and the motor runs below rated speed.
diagrams.caption: Armature-control method for speeds below rated speed

study_groups.heading: Quick comparison
bullets: Above rated speed → field control / flux weakening.
Below rated speed → armature control using a series rheostat.
The direction of change follows from \(N\propto(V-I_aR_a)/\Phi\): decrease \(\Phi\) to raise speed; increase the series armature drop to lower speed.

ai_sections.title: Swinburne’s Test
paragraphs: Swinburne’s test is a no-load test used to predetermine the efficiency of a DC shunt machine as a motor or generator from a small set of no-load measurements.
The idea is to measure the no-load input, separate the armature copper loss from the remaining approximately constant loss, and then use those losses to estimate efficiency at a chosen load.
ai_sections.key_point: Swinburne’s test uses no-load measurements to separate armature copper loss from a constant-loss component, then predetermines motor or generator efficiency at a chosen load.

study_groups.heading: Purpose and test idea
paragraphs: Instead of loading the machine to its full output, run the DC shunt machine as a motor at rated voltage and rated speed on no load, measure the no-load input, and separate the losses. Those losses are then used to predetermine efficiency at chosen motor or generator loads.

study_groups.heading: Test setup and readings
bullets: Use the DC shunt machine in motor operation with its shunt field connected across the supply through a field rheostat.
Measure supply voltage \(V\), no-load line current \(I_{L0}\) and field current \(I_f\) after bringing the machine to rated speed.
The no-load armature current is the line current minus the field current.
paragraphs: The connection diagram belongs here because the first calculation comes directly from the way the no-load line current divides between the shunt field and the armature.

diagrams.title: No-load connection of a DC shunt machine
diagrams.alt: Recommended educational circuit for Swinburne’s no-load test on a DC shunt machine, showing supply voltage measurement, line current measurement, shunt field branch with field rheostat and field-current measurement, and the motor armature.
diagrams.teaching_note: Use the circuit to read the current split before doing the calculation. The line ammeter measures \(I_{L0}\). At the supply node, this current divides into field current \(I_f\) and armature current \(I_{a0}\), so \(I_{a0}=I_{L0}-I_f\). The voltmeter gives the supply voltage \(V\), which is used with \(I_{L0}\) to obtain the no-load input power.

Show a DC supply with a line ammeter measuring I_L0, a voltmeter across the supply, and two parallel machine branches: an armature branch and a shunt-field branch containing the field winding, field rheostat and a field ammeter measuring I_f. Label the armature current I_a0 and make the current relation I_L0 = I_a0 + I_f visually unambiguous. Indicate that the machine is running as a motor on no mechanical load. Do not invent numerical values, meter ranges, source polarity, starter details or protection devices unless they are present in the verified reference. Apply NRS blue-ink notebook styling only after the circuit connectivity has been checked against the chosen reference.
diagrams.caption: Swinburne’s test: no-load DC shunt-machine connection

study_groups.heading: Separate variable and constant losses
steps: Calculate the no-load armature copper loss as \(I_{a0}^2R_a\).
Calculate the no-load input power as \(W_{in,0}=VI_{L0}\).
Subtract the no-load armature copper loss from the no-load input. The remainder is treated as the constant-loss component for the efficiency-prediction sequence.

study_groups.heading: Predetermine efficiency at a chosen load
bullets: For motor operation, calculate the armature copper loss at the chosen armature current, add the constant loss, and subtract total losses from electrical input to obtain output.
For generator operation, calculate total losses at the chosen generator armature current and add them to electrical output to obtain the required mechanical input.
The test is therefore an indirect predetermination method: the machine is not actually supplying the chosen full-load output during the no-load test.

study_groups.heading: Exam-ready sequence
steps: Run the DC shunt machine at rated voltage and rated speed on no load.
Record \(V\), \(I_{L0}\) and \(I_f\).
Find no-load armature copper loss \(I_{a0}^2R_a\).
Find constant loss from no-load input minus no-load armature copper loss.
At the required motor or generator load, add the corresponding armature copper loss to the constant loss and compute efficiency.

ai_sections.title: Three-phase Induction Motor — Types and Construction
pyq_focus: 2023–24 Q7(b) · squirrel-cage vs slip-ring induction motor (5M)
paragraphs: A three-phase induction motor has two main parts: a stationary stator and a rotating rotor. The stator carries a three-phase distributed winding; rotor current is induced rather than supplied directly in normal induction-motor operation.

rows: Three-phase insulated winding connected to slip rings
Can be inserted through slip rings
Starting current/torque can be improved with external resistance
More complex because of brushes and slip rings

ai_sections.key_point: The two rotor constructions are phase-wound (slip-ring) and squirrel-cage. The practical difference is whether the rotor winding is brought out through slip rings so that external rotor resistance can be connected.

study_groups.heading: Basic construction
bullets: A three-phase induction motor has two main parts: a stationary stator and a rotating rotor.
The stator has slots on its inner periphery and carries a three-phase distributed winding.
The rotor core is laminated and has slots for either a rotor winding or conducting rotor bars.
The two rotor constructions required here are phase-wound (slip-ring) and squirrel-cage.

study_groups.heading: Phase-wound / slip-ring rotor
bullets: A three-phase distributed rotor winding is placed in slots on the outer periphery of the rotor and is designed for the same number of poles as the stator winding.
The rotor winding is connected in star or delta.
Three rotor terminals are brought out through three slip rings on the shaft and brushes.
External resistance can therefore be inserted in the rotor circuit to reduce starting current and improve starting torque.
This construction is associated with larger machines where high starting torque is required.

diagrams.title: Phase-wound rotor
diagrams.alt: Figure 4.2 · Phase-wound rotor · Textbook p. 187
diagrams.teaching_note: Read this rotor together with the construction points above. The rotor carries a three-phase winding, and its three terminals are brought to slip rings on the shaft. Stationary brushes make contact with the rings, allowing external resistance to be connected in the rotor circuit during starting.
diagrams.caption: Phase-wound rotor: rotor winding brought out through slip rings

study_groups.heading: Squirrel-cage rotor
bullets: Solid conducting bars are placed in rotor slots and short-circuited by end rings at both ends.
The resulting arrangement resembles a squirrel cage, giving the rotor its name.
The rotor circuit is permanently short-circuited, so external rotor resistance cannot be inserted.
The construction is simple and rugged and has excellent running performance, although its starting performance is poorer than the slip-ring arrangement described above.

diagrams.title: Squirrel-cage rotor
diagrams.alt: Figure 4.4 · Squirrel-cage rotor · Textbook p. 188
diagrams.teaching_note: Here the rotor conductors are bars permanently short-circuited by end rings. There are no slip-ring terminals for inserting external rotor resistance. This is the constructional reason the squirrel-cage rotor is simpler and more rugged.
diagrams.caption: Squirrel-cage rotor: bars permanently short-circuited by end rings

ai_sections.title: Induction Motor Principle, Synchronous Speed and Slip
pyq_focus: 2025–26 Part A(d) · define slip and slip speed (2M)
2025–26 Q7(a) · principle of operation (5M)
2023–24 Q7(a) · principle of operation (5M)
paragraphs: A balanced three-phase supply to the stator produces a rotating magnetic field (RMF). The RMF rotates at synchronous speed. Because the rotor has relative motion with respect to this field, emf and current are induced in the rotor and their interaction with the stator field produces torque.
ai_sections.key_point: Induction requires relative motion. Non-zero slip is therefore necessary for an induction motor to develop torque.

study_groups.heading: Rotating magnetic field and synchronous speed
bullets: A three-phase induction motor is singly excited: electrical supply is applied only to the stator winding.
A balanced three-phase stator supply produces a rotating magnetic field (RMF).
The RMF rotates at synchronous speed, determined by supply frequency and the number of stator poles.

diagrams.title: Production of rotating magnetic field
diagrams.alt: Figure 4.6 · Production of rotating magnetic field · Textbook p. 189
diagrams.teaching_note: Use the drawing to connect the three-phase stator currents with the resultant magnetic field. Although the individual phase currents vary with time, their combined effect is a magnetic field whose axis moves continuously around the air gap. That field rotates at synchronous speed \(N_s\).
diagrams.caption: Three-phase stator currents producing a rotating magnetic field

study_groups.heading: How rotor torque is produced
steps: The rotating stator field sweeps past the rotor conductors.
Relative motion between the RMF and rotor induces rotor emf.
Because the rotor circuit is closed/short-circuited, rotor current flows.
Interaction between the stator field and rotor-current field produces electromagnetic torque.
The rotor therefore accelerates in the direction of the rotating stator field.

diagrams.title: Stator and rotor fluxes
diagrams.alt: Figure 4.7 · Stator and rotor fluxes · Textbook p. 189
diagrams.teaching_note: The rotating stator field cuts the rotor conductors because the rotor is initially moving more slowly than the field. The induced rotor current produces a rotor magnetic effect, and the interaction of stator and rotor fields produces torque in the direction of the rotating field.
diagrams.caption: Stator and rotor magnetic fields involved in induction-motor torque

study_groups.heading: Why the rotor cannot reach synchronous speed
bullets: Rotor emf exists only because there is relative motion between the RMF and the rotor.
If rotor speed became equal to \(N_s\), relative speed would be zero.
Then rotor emf and rotor current would fall to zero, so electromagnetic torque would also disappear.
A motoring induction motor therefore runs slightly below synchronous speed.

study_groups.heading: Slip, slip speed and rotor frequency
bullets: Slip speed is the difference between synchronous speed and actual rotor speed.
Slip \(s\) is that speed difference expressed as a fraction of synchronous speed.
At standstill, \(N=0\) and \(s=1\).
Rotor-current frequency is proportional to slip: it equals supply frequency at standstill and falls as rotor speed approaches synchronous speed.

study_groups.heading: Rotor quantities while running
bullets: If \(E_2\) and \(X_2\) denote standstill rotor emf and leakage reactance, their running values are reduced in proportion to slip.
Rotor resistance \(R_2\) is unchanged in the relation, while the reactance term becomes \(sX_2\).

ai_sections.title: Torque–Slip Characteristics
pyq_focus: 2025–26 Q7(b) · torque–slip characteristics (5M)
paragraphs: The torque changes with slip because rotor emf, rotor frequency and rotor reactance all depend on slip. The characteristic has three important regions/points.
ai_sections.key_point: On the torque–slip characteristic, torque is zero at \(s=0\), rises approximately in proportion to slip in the low-slip region, reaches maximum torque at \(s=R_2/X_2\), and then falls toward the starting point at \(s=1\).

study_groups.heading: Torque expression
paragraphs: Expressing rotor current and rotor power factor in terms of slip gives the torque–slip relation below. It is the starting point for reading the whole torque–slip characteristic.

diagrams.title: Stator and rotor fluxes producing torque
diagrams.alt: Figure 4.8 · Stator and rotor fluxes producing torque · Textbook p. 195
diagrams.teaching_note: This picture is the physical starting point for the torque expression: electromagnetic torque comes from the interaction of the stator field with the rotor field produced by induced rotor current. Slip changes the rotor emf, current and power factor, which is why torque changes with slip.
diagrams.caption: Field interaction that produces induction-motor torque

study_groups.heading: Low-slip region — near synchronous speed
steps: At low slip, \(sX_2\ll R_2\).
Therefore \((sX_2)^2\) is small compared with \(R_2^2\) and may be neglected in the denominator.
The remaining relation gives \(T\propto s\).
Hence torque rises approximately linearly as slip increases from zero.

study_groups.heading: High-slip region — low rotor speed
steps: At high slip, \(sX_2\gg R_2\).
Then \(R_2^2\) is small compared with \((sX_2)^2\).
The torque relation reduces to \(T\propto1/s\).
Hence in this region torque falls as slip becomes larger.

study_groups.heading: Maximum and starting torque
bullets: The torque reaches its maximum when slip satisfies \(s=R_2/X_2\).
At starting, rotor speed is zero and \(s=1\); the torque corresponding to this point is the starting torque.
At synchronous speed, \(s=0\), rotor emf/current vanish and the motor develops no induction torque.

study_groups.heading: Reading the torque–slip curve
bullets: Start from \(s=0\): torque is zero.
In the low-slip region, torque rises nearly in direct proportion to slip.
The curve reaches the maximum-torque point at \(s=R_2/X_2\).
Beyond that point, in the high-slip region, torque decreases approximately as \(1/s\).
Mark the starting point at \(s=1\).

diagrams.title: Torque-slip characteristics
diagrams.alt: Figure 4.9 · Torque-slip characteristics · Textbook p. 196
diagrams.teaching_note: Trace the curve from left to right. At synchronous speed \(s=0\), induction torque is zero. In the low-slip region the curve rises nearly linearly, reaches maximum torque at \(s=R_2/X_2\), and then falls in the high-slip region. The point at \(s=1\) is the starting torque.
diagrams.caption: Torque–slip characteristic with zero, maximum and starting-torque points

ai_sections.title: Synchronous Generator — Working Principle
paragraphs: A synchronous generator (alternator) converts mechanical power into AC electrical power by electromagnetic induction. In the construction used here, the DC-excited field is on the rotor and the armature winding is on the stator.
A prime mover rotates the rotor field. North and South poles sweep past the stationary armature conductors, so the flux linking them alternates and a sinusoidal emf is induced.
ai_sections.key_point: Mechanical rotation of a DC-excited rotor field produces alternating emf in the stationary armature winding.

study_groups.heading: What a synchronous generator does
paragraphs: A synchronous generator, also called an alternator, converts mechanical input power into AC electrical power by electromagnetic induction.

diagrams.title: Synchronous-generator block diagram
diagrams.alt: Figure 4.10 · Synchronous-generator block diagram · Textbook p. 197
diagrams.teaching_note: Use this as the overview of the energy conversion taking place: the machine receives mechanical input from a prime mover and delivers AC electrical output. The remaining blocks below explain how the rotating magnetic field produces that electrical output.
diagrams.caption: Synchronous generator as a mechanical-to-AC energy converter

study_groups.heading: Construction used for the principle
bullets: The field winding is on the rotor and is excited by DC so that the rotor carries magnetic poles.
The armature winding is stationary and distributed in slots around the stator.
A prime mover rotates the field rotor at synchronous speed.

diagrams.title: Cross-sectional view of synchronous machine
diagrams.alt: Figure 4.11 · Cross-sectional view of synchronous machine · Textbook p. 198
diagrams.teaching_note: The important constructional idea in this cross-section is which part moves. The DC-excited field system is on the rotor, while the armature conductors are on the stationary stator. Rotation therefore carries successive North and South rotor poles past the stator conductors.
diagrams.caption: Rotating field rotor and stationary armature of a synchronous generator

study_groups.heading: Working sequence
steps: DC excitation establishes the rotor magnetic field.
The prime mover rotates the rotor.
North and South rotor poles sweep past the stationary stator conductors.
The changing flux linkages induce emf in the stator armature winding by electromagnetic induction.
Successive North and South poles pass a conductor, so the induced emf alternates; with sinusoidally distributed air-gap flux, the generated emf is sinusoidal.

diagrams.title: Sinusoidal generated voltage
diagrams.alt: Figure 4.12 · Sinusoidal generated voltage · Textbook p. 198
diagrams.teaching_note: As successive North and South poles pass a stator conductor, the direction of flux linking the conductor reverses, so the induced emf alternates. With a sinusoidally distributed air-gap flux, the generated voltage follows the sinusoidal waveform shown.
diagrams.caption: Alternating sinusoidal voltage generated as rotor poles pass the stator winding

study_groups.heading: Generated frequency
bullets: For \(P\) poles, one mechanical revolution corresponds to \(P/2\) electrical cycles.
Therefore generated frequency depends directly on rotor speed and pole count.

study_groups.heading: Generated emf
bullets: The emf expression uses flux per pole, generated frequency and turns of the armature winding.
Fleming’s right-hand rule gives the induced-current direction.

ai_sections.title: Voltage Regulation by Synchronous Impedance Method
pyq_focus: 2025–26 Q8 · synchronous-impedance method for alternator voltage regulation (10M)
paragraphs: Voltage regulation compares the internal/no-load generated emf required for a stated load with the terminal voltage. The synchronous-impedance (EMF) method obtains the machine impedance from open-circuit and short-circuit characteristics.
ai_sections.caution: OCC and SCC values must correspond to the same field current, and the voltage/current quantities must be used consistently on a per-phase basis. Keep the stated power-factor phasor convention explicit.
ai_sections.key_point: The method is a sequence: OCC + SCC → \(Z_s\) → \(X_s\) → internal emf \(E_0\) → voltage regulation.

study_groups.heading: What voltage regulation means here
paragraphs: The synchronous-impedance (EMF) method estimates the internal generated emf required to maintain a specified terminal voltage at a stated load current and power factor, and then compares that emf with terminal voltage.

study_groups.heading: Open-circuit characteristic (OCC)
bullets: Run the alternator at rated speed.
Keep the armature open-circuited (no load).
Vary field current and record generated/terminal voltage.
The resulting voltage-versus-field-current curve is the OCC.

study_groups.heading: Short-circuit characteristic (SCC)
bullets: Run the alternator at rated speed with the armature terminals symmetrically short-circuited.
Vary field current and record armature short-circuit current.
The resulting current-versus-field-current curve is the SCC.

study_groups.heading: Find synchronous impedance and reactance
steps: Choose the same field current on the OCC and SCC.
Use consistent per-phase voltage and current values.
Calculate synchronous impedance from open-circuit voltage divided by short-circuit current.
With armature resistance \(R_a\) known, calculate synchronous reactance from \(Z_s^2=R_a^2+X_s^2\).

diagrams.title: Open- and short-circuit characteristics used to obtain synchronous impedance
diagrams.alt: Recommended study diagram showing the open-circuit characteristic and short-circuit characteristic of a synchronous generator against field current, with the same field-current setting used to obtain open-circuit voltage and short-circuit current.
diagrams.teaching_note: The two tests must be read together. Choose one field-current value, read the corresponding open-circuit voltage \(V_{OC}\) from the OCC and short-circuit current \(I_{SC}\) from the SCC, and use those matched readings to calculate \(Z_s=V_{OC}/I_{SC}\).
diagrams.search_query: NPTEL Lecture 90 OC SC Test Synchronous Generator OCC SCC characteristics
diagrams.ai_prompt: Create an NRS educational diagram for the synchronous-impedance (EMF) method using the verified OCC/SCC reference. Show field current on the horizontal axis and clearly distinguish the open-circuit voltage characteristic (OCC) from the short-circuit current characteristic (SCC). Mark one common field-current setting and show that the corresponding V_OC and I_SC readings are taken at that same excitation before forming Z_s = V_OC/I_SC. Do not invent numerical scales, machine ratings, connection details or test values. Preserve the qualitative curve shapes and labels from the chosen verified reference, and apply NRS blue-ink notebook styling only after semantic verification.
diagrams.caption: OCC and SCC readings used to obtain synchronous impedance

study_groups.heading: Find generated emf for the specified load
bullets: Represent the synchronous impedance by \(R_a+jX_s\).
Use the stated load current and power factor in the generator phasor relation.
With a consistent sign/phasor convention, obtain the magnitude of internal generated emf \(E_0\).

study_groups.heading: Complete calculation sequence
steps: OCC at rated speed.
SCC at rated speed.
Same field current → calculate \(Z_s\).
Use \(R_a\) → calculate \(X_s\).
Use load current and power factor → calculate \(E_0\).
Substitute \(E_0\) and \(V\) in the regulation expression.

ai_sections.title: Synchronous Motor — Principle of Operation
paragraphs: A balanced three-phase stator supply produces a rotating magnetic field at synchronous speed. The rotor carries a magnetic field established by DC excitation.

Electromagnetic torque acts between the rotor field and the rotating stator field. When the rotor field locks with the stator field, the rotor follows it at exactly the same speed in steady synchronous operation.
ai_sections.key_point: The defining idea is magnetic locking: rotor field and stator rotating field move together at synchronous speed.

study_groups.heading: Stator magnetic field
bullets: A balanced AC supply is applied to the stator winding.
The stator currents produce a rotating magnetic field.
This stator field rotates at synchronous speed.

study_groups.heading: Rotor magnetic field
bullets: The rotor carries a magnetic field established by DC excitation.
Electromagnetic torque acts between the rotor magnetic field and the rotating stator field.

study_groups.heading: Magnetic locking and synchronous operation
steps: The stator field rotates at \(N_s\).
The rotor field experiences electromagnetic torque that tends to align it with the rotating stator field.
When the rotor field locks with the stator rotating field, the rotor follows that field.
In steady synchronous operation, rotor speed therefore equals synchronous speed.

diagrams.title: Magnetic locking of the DC-excited rotor field with the rotating stator field
diagrams.alt: Recommended educational diagram showing a rotating stator magnetic field and a DC-excited rotor magnetic field locked together and rotating at synchronous speed.
diagrams.teaching_note: Read the picture as two magnetic fields moving together. The stator field rotates at \(N_s\); once the DC-excited rotor field is locked with it, the rotor follows at the same speed. In steady synchronous operation there is therefore no relative speed between the two magnetic fields.
diagrams.search_query: NPTEL Lecture 82 synchronous motor operation rotating magnetic field rotor locking
diagrams.ai_prompt: Create an NRS educational schematic of the basic synchronous-motor operating principle using the verified NPTEL reference. Show a rotating stator magnetic field and a DC-excited rotor with clearly identified North and South poles. Show that, after magnetic locking, the rotor field and stator rotating field move together at the same synchronous speed N_s. Do not add numerical values, detailed phasors, starting arrangements, damper windings, torque-angle values or circuit details unless they are present in the verified reference. Keep the diagram limited to the R25 operating principle and use NRS blue-ink notebook styling after semantic verification.
diagrams.caption: Magnetic locking in a synchronous motor

study_groups.heading: How it differs from induction operation
bullets: In steady synchronous operation, the rotor runs exactly at synchronous speed: \(N=N_s\).
The rotor field and the stator rotating field therefore have no relative speed once they are locked together.
This is different from an induction motor, which requires non-zero slip to induce rotor current and develop torque.

ai_sections.title: Stepper Motor — Principle and Applications
paragraphs: A stepper motor moves through discrete equal angular steps. The rotor can be moved to, and held at, one of these step positions by controlling the sequence in which stator phase groups are energised.
ai_sections.key_point: Sequential excitation converts electrical command pulses into controlled angular position steps.

study_groups.heading: Basic idea
paragraphs: A stepper motor converts an electrical pulse sequence into discrete angular movement. Instead of rotating continuously, the rotor moves through equal angular steps and can be held at a step position.

study_groups.heading: Main types
bullets: Variable-reluctance stepper motor.
Permanent-magnet stepper motor.
Hybrid synchronous stepper motor.

study_groups.heading: Variable-reluctance example — reading the phase groups
bullets: The illustrated stator has six electromagnets forming three phase groups: A–AA, B–BB and C–CC.
An electronic controller energises these groups in sequence.
The rotor always tends to align its teeth with the energised stator magnetic axis because that is the minimum-reluctance position.

diagrams.title: Cross-sectional view of stepper motor
diagrams.alt: Figure 4.13 · Cross-sectional view of stepper motor · Textbook p. 199
diagrams.teaching_note: Use the cross-section to follow the phase-group notation used in the working sequence. A–AA, B–BB and C–CC are the three stator phase groups. When one group is energised, the rotor teeth move toward alignment with that magnetic axis, the minimum-reluctance position.
diagrams.caption: Variable-reluctance stepper motor and its three stator phase groups

study_groups.heading: Step-by-step working
steps: Energise A–AA: the rotor teeth align with the A–AA magnetic axis, which is a minimum-reluctance position.
De-energise A–AA and energise B–BB: the active magnetic axis shifts, so the rotor moves to the next minimum-reluctance position.
In the illustrated example the rotor moves 30° clockwise. That 30° movement is one step, so the step angle in this example is 30°.
Continue the sequence B–BB → C–CC → A–AA to move the rotor through successive equal steps.

study_groups.heading: Applications
bullets: Flatbed/image scanners and computer printers.
3D printers and plotters.
CD drives, intelligent lighting systems and camera lenses.
CNC machines.
Laser/optics positioning such as linear actuators and mirror mounts.
Fluid-control systems.

ai_sections.title: Basic Layout of a Domestic Electrical Installation
pyq_focus: 2025–26 Q9(a) · domestic electrical-installation layout (5M)
paragraphs: In a single-phase domestic installation, the household loads are supplied between phase and neutral at about 230 V. The incoming supply passes through metering, main protection and a distribution board before reaching the final sub-circuits.

diagrams.title: Lay-out of wiring in domestic installations
diagrams.alt: Figure 4.14 · Lay-out of wiring in domestic installations · Textbook p. 201

ai_sections.key_point: Remember the flow: supply → service protection → energy meter → main MCB → distribution board → protected sub-circuits → loads, with earthing of exposed metalwork.

study_groups.heading: Supply used in a domestic installation
bullets: Domestic installations may use single-phase 230 V or three-phase 415 V AC supply.
In a single-phase circuit, the load is connected between phase and neutral and receives about 230 V.

study_groups.heading: Incoming-supply path
steps: Service wire brings phase and neutral from the supply system.
A service fuse is placed in the phase conductor to protect the service wire against overloading.
The supply passes through the energy meter, which records electrical-energy consumption.
From the meter, the supply goes through the main MCB, which controls/protects the whole domestic installation.
The main MCB feeds the distribution board.
The distribution board divides the installation into separate sub-circuits, each protected by its own MCB.

study_groups.heading: Why the distribution board is useful
bullets: Each sub-circuit has its own phase and neutral path and its own protective MCB.
If one sub-circuit is overloaded or short-circuited, its MCB can trip and isolate only that part while unaffected sub-circuits continue to operate.
The stated domestic sub-circuit limit is a maximum of 10 load points and a maximum rating of 800 W; fans, lights and 5 A sockets are counted as load points.

study_groups.heading: Earthing in the layout
bullets: Metallic covers/enclosures of the energy meter, MCBs and distribution board are connected to the earth conductor.
This provides the protective earth path used to reduce electric-shock risk if a live conductor contacts a metal enclosure.

ai_sections.title: Types of Wiring

diagrams.title: Cleat wiring
diagrams.alt: Figure 4.15 · Cleat wiring · Textbook p. 202

diagrams.title: Conduit wiring
diagrams.alt: Figure 4.18 · Conduit wiring · Textbook p. 203

ai_sections.key_point: For short answers, identify each wiring system by its physical method of supporting/protecting the conductors.

study_groups.heading: Cleat wiring
bullets: PVC wires are supported by porcelain cleats consisting of a grooved base and cover.
Cleats are mounted about 6 mm above the wall and spacing between cleats should not exceed 60 cm.
It is cheap and suited to temporary wiring.
Because the conductors are exposed, they are more liable to mechanical injury.

study_groups.heading: Casing-and-capping wiring
bullets: Rectangular casings with grooves are fixed to the wall.
Wires are laid in the grooves and a capping is fixed over the casing.
It gives good appearance and long life.
It provides no safety from fire and requires regular maintenance.

study_groups.heading: TRS / CTS batten wiring
bullets: Uses Tough Rubber Sheath (TRS) or Cab Tyre Sheathed (CTS) wires.
The wires are flexible and resist moisture absorption, chemicals, water and steam.
They are fixed to wooden battens using tinned-brass link clips.
The method is cheap, neat-looking and long-lived, but is not suitable for open areas.

study_groups.heading: Lead- / metal-sheathed wiring
bullets: Uses PVC wires with an outer lead-aluminium alloy sheath (95% lead and 5% aluminium as stated in the source).
The metal sheath protects the conductors against mechanical injury and atmospheric effects.
The wires are fixed on wooden battens using link clips.

study_groups.heading: Conduit wiring
bullets: PVC conduits/pipes carry the wires and give them mechanical enclosure.
Surface conduit: conduits are fixed on the wall with saddles and screws; this arrangement is generally used in workshops and factories.
Concealed conduit: conduits are buried inside walls and plastered; the wiring must be water-tight.
Concealed conduit is widely used in offices and domestic installations, but replacement of a damaged conduit is difficult.

ai_sections.title: Switch Fuse Unit (SFU)
paragraphs: A Switch Fuse Unit is a compact combination of a switch and a fuse, generally enclosed in a metal cover and used at low/medium voltages.
ai_sections.caution: Verified mismatch: SFU is a switch-and-fuse unit. Do not explain SFU using an earth-leakage/current-balance mechanism; earth-leakage protection belongs under ELCB.
ai_sections.key_point: SFU = switch + fuse: control/isolation plus sacrificial over-current protection.

study_groups.heading: Fuse — the protection element inside an SFU
bullets: A fuse is connected in series with the circuit.
Its essential element is a metal strip or wire designed to melt when excessive current flows.
When it melts, the circuit opens and current flow stops.
Short circuit, overloading, mismatched load or device failure can operate the fuse.
After fuse operation, the fuse element must be replaced before the circuit is restored.

study_groups.heading: Switch Fuse Unit
bullets: SFU stands for Switch Fuse Unit.
It combines a switch and fuse in one compact unit, generally inside a metal enclosure.
The switch provides manual switching/isolation; the fuse provides sacrificial over-current protection.
The unit is used at low and medium voltages.

study_groups.heading: Keep the functions separate
bullets: SFU protection is based on the fuse melting under excessive current.
Earth-leakage detection is a different protection function and is treated separately under ELCB.

ai_sections.title: MCB, ELCB and MCCB
pyq_focus: 2024–25 Part A(d) · differentiate MCB and MCCB (2M)
2023–24 Q8(a) · working of MCB (5M)
paragraphs: These three LT protective devices differ mainly in the fault condition they are intended to respond to and the current/fault level of the installation.

rows: Automatically opens for overload and short-circuit conditions; overload tripping uses a bimetal element.
Resettable protection for lower-current final/domestic circuits.
Disconnects supply when an earth-leakage condition indicates an electrical hazard.
Earth-leakage protection; do not treat it as ordinary overload protection.
Protects against overload and short circuit at higher current and fault levels; may have adjustable trip settings.
Used for larger loads, main feeders and industrial distribution.

diagrams.title: MCB
diagrams.alt: Figure 4.24 · MCB · Textbook p. 206

ai_sections.caution: Keep the R25 term ELCB. Do not automatically relabel it as RCCB.
ai_sections.key_point: Over-current/short circuit → MCB or MCCB. Earth leakage → ELCB.

study_groups.heading: MCB — Miniature Circuit Breaker
bullets: An MCB automatically switches OFF the circuit under abnormal conditions such as overload or short circuit.
Unlike a fuse, it is resettable after operation.
For overload protection, the described MCB uses a bimetal element. Heating caused by excessive current bends the bimetal and trips the mechanism.
It is used as resettable over-current protection for lower-current domestic/final circuits.

study_groups.heading: ELCB — Earth Leakage Circuit Breaker
bullets: An ELCB is an earth-leakage protection device.
When an earth-leakage condition creates an electrical hazard, the ELCB disconnects the supply.
Its protective purpose is therefore different from the ordinary overload/short-circuit function of an MCB.
Do not silently replace the term ELCB with RCCB; the R25 wording specifically asks for ELCB.

study_groups.heading: MCCB — Moulded Case Circuit Breaker
bullets: An MCCB is used where load current is above the range of a miniature circuit breaker.
It provides protection against overload and short-circuit faults at higher current and fault levels.
Applications include larger domestic/industrial loads, generator protection and main feeder distribution.
MCCBs may provide discrimination and adjustable overload or earth-fault settings.

study_groups.heading: Fast distinction for revision
bullets: MCB → lower-current resettable overload/short-circuit protection.
ELCB → earth-leakage hazard protection.
MCCB → higher-current/higher-fault-level circuit-breaker protection, often with adjustable settings.

ai_sections.title: Earthing — Need, Pipe Earthing and Plate Earthing
pyq_focus: 2025–26 Q9(b) · need and types of earthing (5M)
2024–25 Q8 · pipe earthing (part of 10M)
2023–24 Q8(b) · define earthing and explain types (5M)
paragraphs: Earthing connects the exposed metallic bodies of electrical equipment to earth through a low-resistance conductor and electrode. If a live conductor touches a metal body, the fault current is given a preferred path to ground instead of through a person.

diagrams.title: Pipe earthing
diagrams.alt: Figure 4.29 · Pipe earthing · Textbook p. 210

diagrams.title: Plate earthing
diagrams.alt: Figure 4.30 · Plate earthing · Textbook p. 210

ai_sections.caution: Verified mismatch: the plate-earthing description contains “G.I. pipe” once, but the subsection and Figure 4.30 identify the electrode as a G.I. plate. Use the plate interpretation.
ai_sections.key_point: The safety purpose is the same in both methods; the difference is the buried earth electrode: pipe versus plate.

study_groups.heading: Definition and need
paragraphs: Earthing (grounding) connects the metallic bodies of electrical equipment to earth through an earth conductor and earth electrode.
bullets: It provides a low-resistance path for leakage/fault current if a live conductor touches a metal body.
It reduces the risk of electric shock to a person touching that metal body.
It reduces fire hazard caused by earth-leakage current.
The source also lists earthing of an alternator neutral as a purpose associated with sustaining generated-system voltage.

study_groups.heading: What happens during an insulation fault
steps: A live conductor accidentally touches the metal body of an appliance.
Because the body is connected to the earth conductor, fault current has a low-resistance path to earth.
The current is diverted away from the person who might touch the body, reducing the danger of electrocution.

study_groups.heading: Pipe earthing
bullets: A G.I. pipe about 38 mm in diameter and 2.5 m long is placed vertically in an earth pit.
The illustrated arrangement uses charcoal and salt around the pipe electrode.
Water is added at regular intervals to maintain moisture and keep earth resistance low.
Pipe earthing is described as the most commonly used earthing system.

study_groups.heading: Plate earthing
bullets: The earth electrode is a G.I. plate of 60 cm × 60 cm × 6 mm.
Charcoal and salt are placed around the plate in alternate layers to reduce earth resistance.
Water is added periodically so that moisture is maintained and earth resistance remains low.

study_groups.heading: Pipe vs plate — one-line distinction
bullets: Both methods serve the same protective purpose; the principal constructional difference is the buried electrode: a vertical G.I. pipe in pipe earthing and a G.I. plate in plate earthing.

ai_sections.title: Classification of Batteries
paragraphs: A battery converts stored chemical energy into electrical energy and may also be used as a backup source when the main supply is interrupted.

rows: Rechargeable; chemical action can be reversed by charging

ai_sections.key_point: Lead-acid is a secondary (rechargeable) battery.

study_groups.heading: Battery idea and use
paragraphs: A battery converts stored chemical energy into electrical energy and consists of electrochemical cells connected to provide the required supply. Batteries can also act as backup sources when the normal power supply is interrupted.
bullets: Applications listed include domestic and medical instruments, electric vehicles, forklifts, flashlights and military use.

study_groups.heading: Primary batteries
bullets: Primary batteries are not rechargeable.
They are intended for single-use discharge.
Dry cell / zinc-carbon battery is the example listed.
As a primary battery is used, its voltage gradually decreases.

study_groups.heading: Secondary batteries
bullets: Secondary batteries are rechargeable.
Their chemical action can be reversed by supplying charging energy.
Examples listed are lead-acid, nickel-cadmium and lithium-ion batteries.
The lead-acid battery studied in this unit is therefore a secondary battery.

ai_sections.title: Lead-Acid Battery — Construction and Working
pyq_focus: 2025–26 Part A(e) · any two advantages of lead-acid battery (2M)
2025–26 Q10 · construction and working of lead-acid battery (part of 10M)
paragraphs: The lead-acid battery is a rechargeable secondary battery used in applications such as automobiles and inverters. It can store a high amount of energy and is described as cheaper and easy to handle, although it is heavy.

diagrams.title: Lead-acid battery
diagrams.alt: Figure 4.31 · Lead-acid battery · Textbook p. 211

ai_sections.key_point: During discharge both plates tend toward lead sulphate and water is formed; charging reverses the chemical process.

study_groups.heading: Construction
bullets: Positive active material: lead dioxide \(PbO_2\).
Negative active material: sponge lead \(Pb\).
Electrolyte: sulphuric acid \(H_2SO_4\) diluted with water in the stated 1:3 proportion.
Separators keep positive and negative plates electrically apart.
The plates and electrolyte are housed in a hard-plastic container.
A cell gives about 2.1 V in the construction discussion; six series-connected cells form a nominal 12 V battery.
Battery capacity is rated in ampere-hours (Ah).

study_groups.heading: Discharge — battery supplying the load
bullets: During discharge, chemical energy is converted into electrical energy.
The positive and negative active materials are converted toward lead sulphate \(PbSO_4\).
Sulphuric acid participates in the reaction and water is formed.

study_groups.heading: Charging — reversing the discharge reaction
bullets: External electrical energy is supplied to the battery.
The discharge chemical reaction is reversed.
Lead and lead dioxide are restored and sulphuric acid is regenerated.

study_groups.heading: Useful construction facts for a descriptive answer
bullets: The battery is a rechargeable secondary battery.
It is commonly used in automobiles and inverters.
It can store a high amount of energy but is physically heavy.

ai_sections.title: Lead-Acid Battery — Electrical Characteristics
pyq_focus: 2023–24 Part A(d) · electrical characteristics of lead-acid battery (2M)
2024–25 Q8(a) · lead-acid battery electrical characteristics (5M)

formulae.label: Ampere-hour efficiency
formulae.latex: \eta_{Ah}=\dfrac{\text{Ah delivered during discharge}}{\text{Ah absorbed during charge}}\times100

diagrams.title: Voltage during charging and discharging
diagrams.alt: Figure 4.32 · Voltage during charging and discharging · Textbook p. 213

diagrams.title: Capacity versus discharge characteristic
diagrams.alt: Figure 4.33 · Capacity versus discharge characteristic · Textbook p. 213

ai_sections.key_point: For R25, remember the three electrical-characteristic headings: voltage, capacity and efficiency.

study_groups.heading: Voltage characteristic
bullets: The fully charged open-circuit cell voltage is stated as about 2.2 V.
Open-circuit voltage depends mainly on how long the cell has been fully charged, electrolyte specific gravity and temperature.
During discharge, terminal voltage falls: the initial change is relatively large and a steadier middle region follows.
The cell voltage should not be allowed to fall below the stated 1.8 V limit because this may increase internal resistance through formation of insoluble lead sulphate.

study_groups.heading: Capacity characteristic
bullets: Battery capacity is specified in ampere-hours (Ah).
Ideal capacity relation: current × discharge time.
For a 100 Ah battery, the source examples are 10 A for 10 h, 20 A for 5 h or 40 A for 2.5 h.
Usable capacity decreases as discharge rate increases; this trend is shown by the capacity-versus-discharge characteristic.

study_groups.heading: Efficiency characteristic
bullets: Two efficiencies are used: ampere-hour efficiency and energy (watt-hour) efficiency.
Ampere-hour efficiency compares charge delivered during discharge with charge absorbed during charging.
The stated ampere-hour efficiency is about 90–95%.
Energy efficiency is always less than ampere-hour efficiency.
Efficiency remains below 100% because of losses such as self-discharge and leakage currents associated with weak insulation.

formulae.label: Ampere-hour efficiency
formulae.latex: \eta_{Ah}=\dfrac{\text{Ah delivered during discharge}}{\text{Ah absorbed during charge}}\times100

study_groups.heading: Three headings to remember
bullets: Voltage → how terminal/open-circuit voltage changes.
Capacity → how much charge can be supplied, in Ah, and the effect of discharge rate.
Efficiency → how much charge/energy is recovered compared with what was put in during charging.

ai_sections.title: UPS — Block Diagram and Operation
pyq_focus: 2025–26 Q10 · UPS operation with block diagram (part of 10M)
paragraphs: An Uninterruptible Power Supply maintains continuity of power for critical AC loads when the normal AC supply is interrupted.

diagrams.title: UPS block diagram
diagrams.alt: Figure 5.44 · UPS block diagram · Textbook p. 243

ai_sections.key_point: The inverter feeds the AC load in both conditions; the DC source changes from rectifier to battery when mains power fails.

study_groups.heading: Purpose of a UPS
paragraphs: An Uninterruptible Power Supply maintains continuity of supply to critical AC loads when the normal AC source is interrupted. It is used where even a temporary loss of power can have serious consequences.

study_groups.heading: Blocks and their roles
bullets: Rectifier: converts the incoming AC supply to DC.
Battery bank: stores DC energy and is connected on the DC link between rectifier and inverter.
Inverter: converts DC back to AC for the critical load.
Filter: conditions/smooths the inverter output before it reaches the load.
Critical load: the equipment whose supply must be maintained.

study_groups.heading: Normal mains available
steps: AC input is applied to the rectifier.
The rectifier produces DC.
That DC supplies the inverter and also charges the battery bank.
The inverter produces AC, which passes through the filter to the critical load.

study_groups.heading: Mains supply fails
steps: The AC input/rectifier supply is no longer available.
The battery bank supplies DC to the inverter through the DC link.
The inverter continues converting DC to AC.
After filtering, the AC output continues to supply the critical load.

study_groups.heading: What the block diagram is showing
bullets: The load is fed from the inverter in both normal and mains-failure conditions.
What changes during failure is the DC source feeding the inverter: rectifier under normal supply, battery when mains power is lost.
The UPS also provides quality power and helps regulate load voltage against input-voltage fluctuations.
